items.title: The middle income trap is real but not universal
items.claim: Many countries that reached middle income status (typically $4,000-$12,000 GDP per capita) have struggled to advance to high income. Which describes the phenomenon best?

options.text: A subset (Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, Thailand) have plateaued; others (South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, more recently Poland) have transitioned successfully. Drivers include education, institutional quality, R&D, and shifting from labour-intensive to knowledge-intensive production
All countries reach high income automatically

items.reveal:
The term was popularised by Indermit Gill and Homi Kharas's 2007 World Bank study. World Bank research (2013, 2018) found about 13 of 101 middle-income economies in 1960 reached high income by 2008.

South Korea's transition from low- to high-income was unusually rapid (1960-2000). It combined export orientation, investment in education and selective industrial policy. Argentina's reversal (from rich to middle income across the 20th century) shows the direction isn't fixed.
items.why: Development outcomes are heterogeneous. Single-factor explanations (geography, institutions, culture) often capture parts of the story but don't generalise.

items.title: Switching costs create lock-in even without monopoly
items.claim: Mobile phone contracts, banking services and software subscriptions all create switching costs. How does this affect competition?

options.text: High switching costs reduce price elasticity, allow price discrimination, and create incumbency advantages; competition can shift from price-on-price to acquisition incentives that don't always benefit existing customers
Switching costs only exist in monopoly

items.reveal:
Klemperer's research (1987 onwards) formalised switching cost economics. UK's Open Banking initiative (2018), CASS (Current Account Switch Service 2013) and Ofcom's text-to-switch (2019) all aim to reduce switching frictions specifically.

The CMA's 2016 retail banking market investigation found switching costs and informational frictions sustained higher prices and weak competition.
items.why: Competition exists on a spectrum shaped by frictions. Policy can target the frictions directly (lower switching costs) rather than only firm conduct.

items.title: The Great Moderation ended in 2008
items.claim: From roughly 1985 to 2007, US and UK output volatility fell substantially compared to earlier decades. What did Ben Bernanke call this period in 2004?

options.text: The Great Moderation — and Bernanke credited a combination of better monetary policy, structural changes (services, JIT) and good luck. The period ended emphatically with the 2008 crisis

items.reveal_title: Stability that turned out not to be
items.reveal:
Bernanke's 2004 speech 'The Great Moderation' attributed reduced volatility to improvements in policy. The 2008 crisis suggested 'good luck' had played a larger role than recognised.

Hyman Minsky's earlier 'financial instability hypothesis' argued that stable periods breed speculative behaviour that ultimately destabilises the system — the 'Minsky moment' became a widely used term after 2008.
items.why: Periods of low volatility can mask growing fragility. Confidence in macroeconomic stability before 2008 was substantial; the consensus was wrong.
